MACRO:

While China’s reactions to U.S. trade assaults were often proportional in the past, its countermeasures now are designed to be more severe, according to WSJ sources. (WSJ)

Chinese President Xi plans to use upcoming meetings to press Trump to move beyond the longstanding policy of strategic ambiguity and formally state that the U.S. “opposes” Taiwan’s independence. Ahead of the expected leaders’ summit, Beijing is considering a significant purchase of American soybeans, a request put forward by Trump. (WSJ)

China’s Commerce Minister struck an optimistic tone on talks with the US, saying Beijing and Washington can find solutions ahead of key trade negotiations between the two countries. (BBG)

Trump said on Thursday all trade talks with Canada were terminated following what he called a fraudulent advertisement in which former and late President Ronald Reagan spoke negatively about tariffs. (RTRS)

Canada will cut the number of vehicles Stellantis and General Motors can import tariff-free into the country in response to the automakers’ plans to reduce their manufacturing footprint. (WSJ)

US Energy Secretary Chris Wright urged the FERC on Thursday to grant expedited reviews for data-center grid connections, according to documents reviewed by Bloomberg News. Under a draft proposed rule those reviews would be limited to 60 days, a seismic shift for a process that currently can drag on for years. (BBG)

The Trump administration is readying a proposal to open almost all US coastal waters to new offshore oil drilling despite opposition from state governors and the president’s previous efforts to close off some of the territory. (BBG)

Japan's core consumer prices rose 2.9% year-on-year in September, as expected and up from the 2.7% rise in August, staying above the central bank's 2% target and keeping alive expectations of a near-term interest rate hike. (RTRS)

Japan's manufacturing sector contracted in October at the fastest pace in 19 months due to a sharper decline in new orders, according to the flash S&P PMI reading. (RTRS)

Japan’s Sanae Takaichi pledged to prioritize tackling a cost-of-living crunch and bolstering defense ahead of a visit by US President Donald Trump next week, in her first address to parliament as prime minister. (BBG)

Japan's new finance minister, Satsuki Katayama, said “We usually draw from higher-than-expected tax revenues and unspent funds from previous budgets to fund extra budgets... But if that’s not enough, we’ll have to issue more government bonds — it can’t be helped if it comes to that”. (BBG)

Satsuki Katayama said she does not see a need to comment on the BoJ's current monetary stance, citing the central bank's commitment to maintaining an accommodative environment. (RTRS)

Satsuki Katayama said she had told U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent that Japan-U.S. relations are "extremely important" in her first teleconference with her U.S. counterpart. (RTRS)

Japan's Nikkei share average rose more than 1% on Friday, driven by index heavyweight tech stocks, and was poised for an eighth weekly gain in nine on expectations for fiscal dove Sanae Takaichi's new government. (RTRS)

Chinese stocks advanced as renewed emphasis on technological self-reliance at a key political gathering and confirmation of the US-China summit supported sentiment. (BBG)

China will seek to maintain a certain rate of growth and expand consumption’s share of the economy "significantly" as authorities draft the next five-year development blueprint, a senior official said on Friday. (BBG)

China needs a bolder spending package to mend the finances of households and companies, according to a central bank adviser, as signs of resilience in the economy mask the damage wrought by the trade war with the US. (BBG)

China plans to sell up to $4 billion dollar-denominated government bonds in Hong Kong, a move that can help create a more reliable yield curve in the offshore market. (BBG)

U.K. retail sales unexpectedly rose in September, helped by tech stores and demand for gold. (WSJ)

The UK's ruling Labour Party suffered a heavy electoral defeat on Friday in Wales, a traditional stronghold, in a result that highlights the threat posed by the Reform UK party, as the government struggles to revive the economy and ease fears about immigration. (RTRS)

The Labour Party remains committed to its pre-election tax pledges, including on income tax, minister Nick Thomas-Symonds told Sky News on Friday, ahead of next month's budget. (Sky News)

British consumer sentiment rose in October to its joint-highest level since August 2024 as shoppers took advantage of sales promotions from Amazon and other retailers, figures from market research company GfK showed on Friday. (RTRS)

Nigel Farage suggested he would replace BoE Governor Bailey if he became prime minister, in a signal the populist leader would interfere in the central bank’s independence if his Reform UK wins the next election. (BBG)

The cyberattack that crippled Jaguar Land Rover Automotive Plc caused British car production to plunge 27% last month, piling more pressure on the country’s beleaguered industry. (BBG)

The European Central Bank will keep euro-zone borrowing costs at 2% through 2027, according to a Bloomberg survey of economists. (BBG)

German private-sector activity unexpectedly jumped to its highest level since May 2023, putting Europe’s biggest economy on a firm footing at the start of the fourth quarter. (BBG)

France’s private sector unexpectedly contracted as wrangling over the budget prolonged fiscal uncertainty for Europe’s second-largest economy. (BBG)

Alberta’s government kicked off a new legislative session pledging to build new pipelines and deploy its vast natural gas reserves to become a major player in artificial intelligence. (BBG)

RBA Governor Bullock highlighted four key areas of focus in work between policymakers, the government and industry to modernize the nation’s payments system, while reiterating the importance of security. (BBG)

Asia may see its resilience to U.S. tariffs challenged if a rally in the dollar and a rebound in low interest rates lead to tighter financial conditions, a senior International Monetary Fund official told Reuters. (RTRS)

No US trade agreements are expected to be signed with Vietnam, Indonesia and the Philippines at the APEC summit, according to Bloomberg sources. (BBG)

South Korea and the US remain “sharply” divided over the cash portion of a $350 billion investment pledge, South Korea’s Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said Friday, hinting that a deal may not be reached in time for a summit meeting. (BBG)

South Korea pledged to take action if needed to stabilize markets after the won declined to a six-month low. (BBG)

Brazil President Lula said he expects to meet with President Trump in Malaysia this weekend to discuss any topic, including the US administration’s controversial use of military strikes against alleged drug shipments coming from Venezuela. (BBG)

India’s overall economic activity slowed in October as services lost pace and demand for new orders softened after higher US tariffs took effect, a flash survey by HSBC Holdings Plc showed. (BBG)

Investors in Turkey are awaiting yet another court verdict on the fate of the main opposition party on Friday, in a case that could once again escalate political tensions in the country. (BBG)

Vietnam’s coffee output in 2025-26 is expected to be 10% higher than the previous crop year if weather conditions remain favorable, an industry group said on Friday. (BBG)

GEOPOLITICAL:

Trump chose a middle-option sanctions plan for Russia, leaving more severe measures and military aid such as Tomahawk missiles for Ukraine off the table, according to WSJ sources. (WSJ)

Trump said “the land is going to be next” in his campaign to halt the flow of drugs into the US from Venezuela, the clearest indication yet that he’s preparing to broaden strikes that have so far been limited to targets at sea. (BBG)

The U.S. flew Air Force B-1 bombers near Venezuela on Thursday, stepping up pressure on President Nicolás Maduro only days after other American warplanes carried out an “attack demonstration” near the South American country. (WSJ)

EQUITIES:

Intel shares rose nearly 10% in Frankfurt on Friday, a day after the company beat expectations for its third quarter profit helped by dramatic cost cutting measures. (RTRS)

Ford Motor cut its profit guidance on Thursday, citing fallout from a fire at a critical aluminum supplier that will crimp production of some of its most lucrative vehicles through the end of the year. (RTRS)

Applied Materials Inc., the largest US producer of chipmaking equipment, plans to cut 4% of its global workforce as it copes with a sales slowdown and trade turmoil. (BBG)

Alphabet Inc.’s Google will supply up to 1 million of its specialized AI chips to Anthropic PBC, a deal worth tens of billions of dollars that deepens its partnership with the fast-growing artificial intelligence startup. (BBG)

Google's tensor processing units are gaining momentum outside the company as a way to train and run complex AI models, with Anthropic PBC unveiling a deal to supply the startup with additional computing power. (BBG)

TSMC’s 2nm wafers are so expensive that the A20 chip set for Apple’s iPhone 18 may cost US$280 each, much higher than the A18’s $45, making it the most expensive component in the iPhone 18. (Mac Rumours)

Newmont Corp. delivered stronger-than-expected quarterly earnings as the world’s largest gold miner started to reap the benefits of cost-cutting measures at a time of surging prices. (BBG)

Rivian Automotive agreed to pay $250 million to settle a 2022 class-action lawsuit that alleged the company’s initial public offering documents made false statements about how much its electric vehicles would cost. (WSJ)

Taiwan’s semiconductor industry output will grow 22% this year to NT$6.5 trillion (US$211 B), as it remains No. 1 in packaging and No.2 in chip design, said Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association Chair Cliff Hou, media report. (CN Yes via @dnystedt)

Power outages of any size can cause “significant financial losses and damage to sensitive manufacturing processes” among semiconductor makers, and the Taiwan Semiconductor Industry Association (TSIA) called on Taipei to shore up the quality, reliability and “green” of energy, media report. (Asian press via @dnystedt) 

China’s State Administration for Market Regulation has visited the offices of the country’s leading food-delivery platforms as part of an investigation into their practices, according to a report by the Economic Observer. (BBG)

Tokyo Gas Co. has signed a preliminary agreement to explore buying liquefied natural gas from a long-stalled project in Alaska that has been championed by Donald Trump, days ahead of a visit by the US president to Japan. (BBG)

Sanofi said robust pharmaceutical launches and increased demand for its blockbuster Dupixent drug drove higher sales and adjusted earnings for the third quarter. (WSJ)

Safran raised its full-year outlook after third-quarter revenue climbed on growth across all its businesses, but forecast that tariffs would lead to a residual hit on its bottom line. (WSJ)

UBS Group named Beatriz Martin, head of noncore assets, new chief operating officer in a reshuffle of its executive team as the bank nominated compliance chief Markus Ronner as vice chairman of its board. (WSJ)

Eni increased its full-year buyback commitment after raising its cost-savings target, as third-quarter earnings rose with higher production offsetting weaker oil prices. (WSJ)

US regulators approved GSK Plc’s blood cancer drug, a decision that will allow the company to bring the medicine back to the world’s biggest pharmaceutical market after questions about its effectiveness led to its withdrawal in 2022. (BBG)

NatWest Group raised its revenue and profitability guidance for the second time this year after strong customer activity helped its third-quarter results top market expectations. (WSJ)

Australian Strategic Materials Ltd. aims to choose a location for its planned US rare earths plant by the end of this year, capitalizing on President Donald Trump’s backing for the sector amid growing rivalry with China. (BBG)

The chief executive of Pilbara Minerals, one of the world’s biggest lithium miners, praised a new critical minerals deal between the U.S. and Australia as a fillip to building out global supply chains for commodities essential to modern technologies. (WSJ)

In the #Philippines, geography is destiny — and a challenge. Over 7,000 islands make up the country, each with its own energy needs and infrastructure gaps. That fragmentation, along with fuel price fluctuations and foreign exchange risks, drives some of Asia’s highest electricity prices (second only to Singapore) and leaves remote communities reliant on imported diesel.

Yet the Philippines is rich in renewable potential, including solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal (due to its location on the Pacific Ring of Fire).

Despite this, fossil fuels still supply 77.7% of its power, with coal alone at 62.5%. Additionally, coal plant breakdowns cause an average of 28 blackouts per household per year, according to a 2024 report. Transmission bottlenecks, investment risks, and regulatory uncertainty continue to slow the rollout of renewables.

Still, momentum is building. The government aims to double the share of renewables to 50% by 2040, attract foreign investment, and expand off-grid hybrid systems to reach islands beyond the main grid. Partnerships with France and Japan are also exploring green hydrogen and offshore wind — a first for Southeast Asia’s typhoon belt.

The Philippines’ energy story is one of contrasts:

⚡ Abundant potential but uneven access

🌍 Ambitious goals but fragmented infrastructure

💨 Rising demand in a country on the frontlines of climate risk

The path to net zero here won’t be linear — but it could offer vital lessons for every region where clean energy must cross water before it reaches people.
